rationale: B wins because it has the discipline to keep three real shapes and make the missing proof painfully explicit. Its strongest line, "Perplexity starts paying the publishers it's been fighting," is the cleanest newsroom conflict here, and it immediately asks for named enrolled publishers and payout mechanics. A is useful, but "Perplexity's new revenue streams are the receipts its last valuation is betting on" starts dressing a thin investor thesis in a sharper suit than the facts earned.
gaps_in_A: "The publishers threatening Perplexity with lawsuits are the same ones it's now offering to pay" overclaims the facts; the update does not say the threatening publishers are eligible, enrolled, or being paid.
"subscription revenue alone hasn't proven out for AI answer engines" is outside the supplied update. It may be true context, but this exercise demanded traceable facts.
"Perplexity's new revenue streams are the receipts its last valuation is betting on" turns a recent valuation into an investor thesis without an investor, round detail, or revenue evidence.

"Perplexity won't say how much publishers actually get paid" is a fair tension, but as a standalone angle it overlaps hard with the publisher-conflict story unless there is publisher reaction or a comparable deal benchmark.
gaps_in_B: "Perplexity starts paying the publishers it's been fighting" still asserts the critic publishers are the payees before proving enrollment or eligibility.
"category-creation" is a little inflated for a shopping launch with no merchants, categories, fee structure, or transaction data disclosed.
"there is no story until a real number exists" is too absolute; undisclosed payout terms can be a legitimate accountability angle if paired with publisher reaction or comparable deal terms.
It underuses the valuation fact. Refusing an "AI bubble" take is correct, but a tighter VC/business-model angle tied to the multi-billion valuation could still work with investor proof.
